example_sentences.en: I would like to pay, please.
Can I pay by card?

cloze.en: We have already paid the bill.

words.notes: Inseparable be- prefix, so no ge- in the participle: hat bezahlt. 'Zahlen' alone works too: 'Zahlen, bitte!'
words.mnemonic: be-ZAHL-en — 'Zahl' is a number, and paying is about numbers.
words.germany_context: Plenty of bakeries, kiosks, doctors' practices and small restaurants are still cash-only. Always ask 'Karte oder bar?' and keep cash on you.

example_sentences.en: How much does that cost?

example_sentences.de: Die Fahrkarte kostet drei Euro fünfzig.
example_sentences.en: The ticket costs three euros fifty.

cloze.en: How much does a coffee cost here?

words.notes: 'Was kostet das?' is the single most useful shopping question. Stem ends in -st, so du kostest.
words.germany_context: Prices on German shelves and menus always include Mehrwertsteuer — the number you see is exactly what you pay at the till.

example_sentences.en: I am selling my old bike.
The shop only sells organic products.

cloze.de: Er hat sein Auto letzte Woche ___.
cloze.en: He sold his car last week.

words.notes: Same family as 'kaufen'; the ver- prefix flips the direction.
words.germany_context: Kleinanzeigen (the old eBay Kleinanzeigen) is where almost everyone in Germany buys and sells used furniture, bikes and electronics — handy when you furnish a first flat.

example_sentences.en: I'm ordering a pizza.
Have you ordered yet?

cloze.en: What are you ordering to drink?

words.notes: Used both for restaurants and for online shopping.
words.germany_context: Tap water is not served in German restaurants. If you order 'Wasser' you get a paid bottle — say 'still' for flat or 'mit Kohlensäure' for sparkling.

example_sentences.en: I'm looking for the train station.

example_sentences.de: Wir suchen eine Wohnung in Berlin.
example_sentences.en: We are looking for a flat in Berlin.

cloze.en: What are you looking for?

words.notes: 'Ich suche …' is the polite opener when you need help in a shop or on the street.
words.germany_context: Flat hunting runs on ImmoScout24 and WG-Gesucht. Bring a Schufa-Auskunft, your last three payslips and a Mieterselbstauskunft to every viewing — landlords expect the full folder.

example_sentences.en: May I use your phone?

example_sentences.de: Ich benutze die App jeden Tag.
example_sentences.en: I use the app every day.

cloze.en: We don't use a car at home.

words.notes: Southern Germany and Austria also say 'benützen'. 'Nutzen' means the same but sounds more formal.

example_sentences.en: I forgot my key.
Don't forget to take out the rubbish.

cloze.en: You always forget my birthday.

words.notes: Strong verb, e→i: du vergisst, er vergisst. The participle has no -t and looks like the infinitive: vergessen.
words.germany_context: Locking yourself out is an expensive mistake here — a Schlüsseldienst call-out easily runs 100–200 €, more at night or on Sunday.

example_sentences.de: Ich erinnere mich an unseren ersten Tag in Berlin.
example_sentences.en: I remember our first day in Berlin.
Do you remember him?

cloze.de: Sie ___ sich nicht an das Passwort.
cloze.en: She doesn't remember the password.

words.notes: Reflexive and always with 'an + Akkusativ'. Without 'sich' it means to remind someone: 'Erinnere mich bitte an den Termin.'

example_sentences.en: You have to decide for yourself.

example_sentences.de: Wir haben uns für die kleine Wohnung entschieden.
example_sentences.en: We decided on the small flat.

cloze.en: I can't make up my mind.

words.notes: 'Sich entscheiden für + Akkusativ' = to decide on something. Strong: entschied, entschieden.

example_sentences.de: Können Sie mir das bitte erklären?
example_sentences.en: Could you please explain that to me?
The teacher explains the grammar.

cloze.en: I'll explain the way to you.

words.notes: 'Jemandem etwas erklären' — the person is dative, the thing accusative.
words.mnemonic: 'klar' is inside erKLÄRen — you make something clear.

example_sentences.en: Please answer me quickly.

example_sentences.de: Er antwortet nie auf meine E-Mails.
example_sentences.en: He never replies to my emails.

cloze.en: Why aren't you answering?

words.notes: 'Jemandem antworten' (Dativ), but 'auf eine Frage antworten'. 'Beantworten' takes a plain accusative: 'eine Frage beantworten'.

example_sentences.en: Could you please repeat that?

example_sentences.de: Ich wiederhole die Vokabeln jeden Abend.
example_sentences.en: I revise the vocabulary every evening.

cloze.de: Der Lehrer ___ den Satz noch einmal.
cloze.en: The teacher repeats the sentence once more.

words.notes: Inseparable in this meaning (ich wiederhole), so no ge- in the participle: hat wiederholt.
words.germany_context: 'Können Sie das bitte wiederholen?' or 'Wie bitte?' are the polite ways to say you didn't catch something — a bare 'Was?' sounds rude.

example_sentences.en: I practise German every day.

example_sentences.de: Wir üben zusammen für die Prüfung.
example_sentences.en: We're practising together for the exam.

cloze.en: You have to practise more!

words.notes: 'Übung macht den Meister' — practice makes perfect.

example_sentences.en: She studies computer science in Munich.
Where did you study?

cloze.en: My brother studies medicine.

words.notes: 'Studieren' means being at university. For school homework or a language, use 'lernen'. Verbs in -ieren never take ge- in the participle.
words.germany_context: Public universities charge no tuition — only a Semesterbeitrag of roughly 150–350 €, which usually includes a regional transport ticket.

example_sentences.de: Ich schicke dir die Adresse per WhatsApp.
example_sentences.en: I'll send you the address by WhatsApp.

example_sentences.de: Kannst du mir ein Foto schicken?
example_sentences.en: Can you send me a photo?

cloze.de: Er hat mir gestern eine E-Mail ___.
cloze.en: He sent me an email yesterday.

words.notes: The everyday word; 'senden' is the formal twin.
words.germany_context: A Päckchen or Paket normally travels with DHL. If nobody is home it goes to a Packstation, a Paketshop or a neighbour — check the yellow slip in your Briefkasten.

example_sentences.de: Wir senden Ihnen die Rechnung per E-Mail.
example_sentences.en: We'll send you the invoice by email.

example_sentences.de: Bitte senden Sie das Formular an das Amt.
example_sentences.en: Please send the form to the office.

cloze.en: I've already sent the file.

words.notes: More formal than 'schicken'. Two past sets: weak sendete/gesendet (everyday, broadcasting) and strong sandte/gesandt (formal letters).

example_sentences.en: I get no signal here.
The boss welcomes the guests.

cloze.en: I didn't receive your message.

words.notes: Strong with Umlaut: du empfängst, er empfängt. In everyday speech people say 'bekommen' or 'kriegen'.

example_sentences.en: I'm booking the hotel online.

example_sentences.de: Wir haben zwei Tickets nach Istanbul gebucht.
example_sentences.en: We booked two tickets to Istanbul.

cloze.en: Have you booked the flight yet?

words.notes: Used for travel, hotels and courses; for a restaurant table Germans say 'reservieren'.
words.germany_context: Deutsche Bahn tickets are far cheaper as a Sparpreis booked weeks ahead, but that ticket only works on the one train you booked.

example_sentences.de: Ich möchte einen Tisch für zwei Personen reservieren.
example_sentences.en: I'd like to reserve a table for two.

example_sentences.de: Wir haben für acht Uhr reserviert.
example_sentences.en: We have a reservation for eight o'clock.

cloze.de: Können Sie mir bitte einen Platz ___?
cloze.en: Could you reserve a seat for me, please?

words.notes: Verb in -ieren: no ge- in the participle.
words.germany_context: In the ICE a Sitzplatzreservierung costs about 5,50 € extra. Without one you can end up standing on busy Friday and Sunday trains.

example_sentences.de: Wir mieten eine Wohnung mit zwei Zimmern.
example_sentences.en: We're renting a two-room flat.

example_sentences.de: Man kann hier auch ein Auto mieten.
example_sentences.en: You can also rent a car here.

cloze.de: Ich habe das Zimmer für drei Monate ___.
cloze.en: I rented the room for three months.

words.notes: 'Mieten' = to rent from someone, 'vermieten' = to rent out. Der Mieter is the tenant, der Vermieter the landlord.
words.germany_context: Budget for a Kaution of up to three months' Kaltmiete plus monthly Nebenkosten (heating, water, rubbish) on top of the rent itself.

example_sentences.de: Ich putze am Samstag die Wohnung.
example_sentences.en: I clean the flat on Saturdays.
Please brush your teeth.

cloze.en: Who is cleaning the bathroom today?

words.notes: Stem ends in -tz, so du and er look the same: du putzt, er putzt.
words.germany_context: Many buildings run a Putzplan or Kehrwoche: tenants take turns cleaning the stairwell and sweeping the pavement. Skipping your week is a genuine neighbour dispute.

example_sentences.en: I'm washing my hands.
Are you doing the laundry today?

cloze.en: He washes the car every Saturday.

words.notes: Strong with Umlaut: du wäschst, er wäscht; past wusch, gewaschen.
words.germany_context: Many buildings share a Waschküche in the cellar with a booking sheet, and running a machine after 22:00 breaks the Nachtruhe.

example_sentences.en: Today I'm cooking Turkish food.
The water is already boiling.

cloze.en: What are you cooking for dinner?

words.notes: Also used intransitively for boiling water.
words.germany_context: Supermarkets are closed all day Sunday, so do the shopping for anything you plan to cook by Saturday evening.

example_sentences.en: My mother is baking a cake.
We baked bread yesterday.

cloze.en: I'm baking cookies for Christmas today.

words.notes: The old strong forms 'du bäckst / er bäckt' still exist but 'backst / backt' is normal today. The participle stays strong: gebacken.
words.germany_context: The Bäckerei is the one shop type usually allowed to open on Sunday mornings — often the only place to buy anything before Monday.

example_sentences.en: I'm cutting the bread.

example_sentences.de: Er hat sich in den Finger geschnitten.
example_sentences.en: He cut his finger.

cloze.en: Can you chop the onions small?

words.notes: Strong: schnitt, geschnitten. 'Sich die Haare schneiden lassen' = to get a haircut.

example_sentences.en: Can you fix my bike?
The heating will be repaired tomorrow.

cloze.en: Who repaired the fridge?

words.notes: Verb in -ieren: no ge- in the participle.
words.germany_context: For anything broken in a rented flat, tell the Hausmeister or write to the Vermieter — repairs to the building and its fittings are the landlord's job, not the tenant's.

example_sentences.en: They're building a new house.
A bridge is being built here.

cloze.de: Die Kinder ___ eine Burg aus Sand.
cloze.en: The children are building a sandcastle.

words.notes: 'Die Baustelle' (building site) is on every second German street sign.

example_sentences.en: I need to change money.

example_sentences.de: Wir wechseln in Frankfurt den Zug.
example_sentences.en: We change trains in Frankfurt.

cloze.en: He changes jobs often.

words.notes: Verbs in -eln drop the e in the ich-form: ich wechsle.
words.germany_context: Switching your Stromanbieter, Handyvertrag or Krankenkasse is completely normal in Germany and usually saves money — but always kündigen in writing before the contract auto-renews.

example_sentences.en: I'd like to change my appointment.
The weather changes quickly.

cloze.en: Can you change the address online?

words.notes: 'Etwas ändern' = to change something; 'sich ändern' = to change by itself.
words.germany_context: A change of address or surname has to be reported separately to the Bürgeramt, your bank, the Krankenkasse and the Finanzamt — nothing updates automatically.

example_sentences.en: Shall we swap seats?

example_sentences.de: Ich tausche meine Schicht mit einem Kollegen.
example_sentences.en: I'm swapping my shift with a colleague.

cloze.en: We exchanged phone numbers.

words.notes: For returning goods to a shop Germans say 'umtauschen'.

example_sentences.en: We're saving up for a flat.
That way you save a lot of time.

cloze.en: I save two hundred euros every month.

words.notes: Works for money and for time or energy alike.
words.germany_context: Germans separate the Girokonto (daily money) from a Tagesgeldkonto (savings). Many banks charge Kontoführungsgebühren, so compare before opening one.

example_sentences.de: Wie viel verdienst du im Monat?
example_sentences.en: How much do you earn a month?
She earns well as an engineer.

cloze.de: Er ___ nicht genug für diese Miete.
cloze.en: He doesn't earn enough for this rent.

words.notes: Also means 'to deserve': 'Du hast eine Pause verdient.'
words.germany_context: German salaries are quoted brutto per year. After Lohnsteuer, Krankenversicherung and the rest, your netto is roughly 60–65 % of that number.

example_sentences.de: Ich gebe zu viel Geld für Essen aus.
example_sentences.en: I spend too much money on food.

example_sentences.de: Wie viel hast du dafür ausgegeben?
example_sentences.en: How much did you spend on that?

cloze.de: Wir ___ jeden Monat 400 Euro für Lebensmittel aus.
cloze.en: We spend 400 euros a month on groceries.

words.notes: Separable and strong: du gibst aus, er gibt aus. 'Ich gebe einen aus' means 'the drinks are on me'.

example_sentences.de: Kannst du mir zehn Euro leihen?
example_sentences.en: Can you lend me ten euros?

example_sentences.de: Ich habe mir ein Buch aus der Bibliothek geliehen.
example_sentences.en: I borrowed a book from the library.

cloze.en: He's lending me his car.

words.notes: 'Jemandem etwas leihen' = to lend; 'sich etwas leihen' = to borrow. Strong: lieh, geliehen.
words.germany_context: A Stadtbibliothek card costs around 10–20 € a year and lets you borrow books, e-books, films and in some cities even tools and board games.

example_sentences.de: Ich borge dir gern mein Fahrrad.
example_sentences.en: I'm happy to lend you my bike.

example_sentences.de: Darf ich mir deinen Stift borgen?
example_sentences.en: May I borrow your pen?

cloze.de: Sie hat sich Geld von ihrem Bruder ___.
cloze.en: She borrowed money from her brother.

words.notes: Same idea as 'leihen' but more colloquial; 'leihen' is the safer everyday choice.

example_sentences.de: Ich schenke ihr Blumen zum Geburtstag.
example_sentences.en: I'm giving her flowers for her birthday.

example_sentences.de: Was hast du deinem Vater geschenkt?
example_sentences.en: What did you give your father?

cloze.en: My parents are giving me a bike.

words.notes: 'Jemandem etwas schenken' — person dative, gift accusative. 'Das Geschenk' is the present.
words.germany_context: If you're invited to a German home, bring a small gift — flowers, wine, or something from your home country. Turning up empty-handed is noticed.

example_sentences.en: Happy birthday!
We congratulate you on your wedding.

cloze.en: Everyone congratulates him on the new job.

words.notes: Dative person plus 'zu + Dativ' for the occasion: 'jemandem zu etwas gratulieren'.
words.germany_context: Germans consider it bad luck to congratulate before the actual day — never say 'Herzlichen Glückwunsch' the evening before someone's birthday.

example_sentences.en: We're celebrating tonight.

example_sentences.de: Sie hat ihren Geburtstag im Park gefeiert.
example_sentences.en: She celebrated her birthday in the park.

cloze.en: What are you celebrating?

words.notes: 'Feierabend' is the end of the working day, not a party.
words.germany_context: At work and among friends the birthday person brings the cake and pays for the round — the opposite of what most newcomers expect.

example_sentences.de: Am Wochenende besuche ich meine Familie.
example_sentences.en: I'm visiting my family at the weekend.

example_sentences.de: Hast du schon das Museum besucht?
example_sentences.en: Have you visited the museum yet?

cloze.en: When are you finally going to visit us?

words.notes: Also 'einen Kurs besuchen' = to attend a course.
words.germany_context: Dropping by unannounced is unusual in Germany. Text or call first, even with close friends and even for neighbours.

example_sentences.en: I'd like to meet new people.

example_sentences.de: Wir haben uns in Berlin kennengelernt.
example_sentences.en: We met in Berlin.

cloze.en: Pleased to meet you!

words.notes: Written as one word but still separable: 'Ich lerne ihn kennen.' The zu goes inside: kennenzulernen.
words.germany_context: A handshake is still standard when meeting someone new, at work and privately. Say your surname clearly — Germans introduce themselves by it.

example_sentences.de: Wir haben uns für Freitag verabredet.
example_sentences.en: We arranged to meet on Friday.

example_sentences.de: Ich verabrede mich oft mit Kollegen nach der Arbeit.
example_sentences.en: I often arrange to meet colleagues after work.

cloze.en: Are you meeting up with her tomorrow?

words.notes: Reflexive, with 'mit + Dativ' for the person. 'Die Verabredung' is the arrangement itself.
words.germany_context: Germans plan private meetings days or weeks ahead. A spontaneous 'let's meet in an hour' rarely works, even with good friends.

example_sentences.en: Can we postpone the appointment?

example_sentences.de: Das Meeting wurde auf Montag verschoben.
example_sentences.en: The meeting was moved to Monday.

cloze.de: Wir haben die Reise auf nächstes Jahr ___.
cloze.en: We postponed the trip to next year.

words.notes: Strong: verschob, verschoben. Also literal: 'den Schrank verschieben' = to shift the cupboard.
words.germany_context: Moving a Termin at an Amt usually means going back to the end of the queue — the next free slot can be weeks or months away.

example_sentences.en: How long does the journey take?
That only takes five minutes.

cloze.en: The film lasts two hours.

words.notes: Used almost only in the 3rd person, so there is no real imperative. 'Es dauert noch' = it'll be a while yet.
words.germany_context: Getting a slot at the Ausländerbehörde can dauern for months. Book the Termin the moment you know you will need one.

example_sentences.en: Hurry up, the bus is coming!
I have to hurry.

cloze.de: Wir ___ uns, sonst kommen wir zu spät.
cloze.en: We're hurrying, otherwise we'll be late.

words.notes: Always reflexive. 'Eile' means haste — 'Beeil dich!' is the everyday 'hurry up!'

example_sentences.en: Someone rang the doorbell.
Please ring twice.

cloze.en: My alarm clock rings at six o'clock.

words.notes: Verbs in -eln drop the e in the ich-form: ich klingle.
words.germany_context: Your surname must be on the Klingelschild and the Briefkasten. Without it, post and parcels get sent straight back to the sender.

example_sentences.en: Please press this button.
The shoes pinch.

cloze.de: Man muss die Tür ___, nicht ziehen.
cloze.en: You have to push the door, not pull it.

words.notes: Also 'jemandem die Daumen drücken' = to keep your fingers crossed for someone.
words.germany_context: German doors are labelled 'Drücken' (push) and 'Ziehen' (pull). Worth memorising before your first Bäckerei door at 7 a.m.

example_sentences.de: Das Kind zieht seine Mutter am Arm.
example_sentences.en: The child is pulling its mother by the arm.

example_sentences.de: Der Zahnarzt hat mir einen Zahn gezogen.
example_sentences.en: The dentist pulled one of my teeth.

cloze.en: You have to pull this door.

words.notes: With 'haben' when you pull something; with 'sein' when it means to move house: 'Er ist nach Köln gezogen.' Strong: zog, gezogen.

example_sentences.de: Wir schieben das Fahrrad den Berg hoch.
example_sentences.en: We're pushing the bike up the hill.

example_sentences.de: Kannst du den Tisch ein bisschen schieben?
example_sentences.en: Can you push the table a bit?

cloze.de: Er hat den Einkaufswagen zur Kasse ___.
cloze.en: He pushed the shopping trolley to the till.

words.notes: 'Schieben' is pushing something along a surface; 'drücken' is pressing against it. Strong: schob, geschoben.

example_sentences.en: Throw the ball to me!

example_sentences.de: Er wirft die Flasche in den Müll.
example_sentences.en: He's throwing the bottle in the bin.

cloze.de: Papier ___ man in die blaue Tonne.
cloze.en: You throw paper in the blue bin.

words.notes: Strong, e→i: du wirfst, er wirft, wirf!; warf, geworfen.
words.germany_context: Mülltrennung is taken seriously: paper in the blue bin, packaging in the yellow one, food waste in brown, the rest in black. Pfand bottles go back to the shop, never in the bin.

example_sentences.en: The goalkeeper catches the ball.

example_sentences.de: Wir haben im Urlaub einen Fisch gefangen.
example_sentences.en: We caught a fish on holiday.

cloze.en: She catches the cat in the garden.

words.notes: Strong with Umlaut: du fängst, er fängt; fing, gefangen. The prefixed 'anfangen' (to begin) is far more common in daily life.

example_sentences.en: Careful, you're going to fall!

example_sentences.de: Das Glas ist auf den Boden gefallen.
example_sentences.en: The glass fell on the floor.

cloze.en: A lot of snow falls here in winter.

words.notes: Strong with Umlaut: du fällst, er fällt; fiel, ist gefallen. Perfekt with 'sein' — it's a change of place.

example_sentences.en: Prices rise every year.

example_sentences.de: Wir sind in den falschen Zug gestiegen.
example_sentences.en: We got on the wrong train.

cloze.en: The rent has gone up again.

words.notes: The base for all the transport verbs: einsteigen (get on), aussteigen (get off), umsteigen (change trains).
words.germany_context: On the S-Bahn and U-Bahn you constantly hear 'Umsteigen zur Linie …' — that is steigen with a prefix, and it's the announcement that matters.

example_sentences.en: Temperatures are falling.
Prices have gone down again.

cloze.de: Im Winter ___ die Temperatur oft unter null.
cloze.en: In winter the temperature often drops below zero.

words.notes: Strong: sank, ist gesunken. Used for prices, temperatures and ships.

example_sentences.en: The children are growing so fast.
Tomatoes grow in the garden.

cloze.en: My hair grows very slowly.

words.notes: Strong with Umlaut: du wächst and er wächst look identical; wuchs, ist gewachsen.

example_sentences.de: Meine Großmutter ist letztes Jahr gestorben.
example_sentences.en: My grandmother died last year.
The plant dies without water.

cloze.en: I'm starving!

words.notes: Strong, e→i: du stirbst, er stirbt; starb, ist gestorben. 'Ich sterbe vor Hunger' = I'm starving.

example_sentences.en: I was born in Izmir in 1993.

example_sentences.de: Unser Sohn ist in Berlin geboren worden.
example_sentences.en: Our son was born in Berlin.

cloze.en: When were you born?

words.notes: In everyday German use the short sein-form: 'Ich bin … geboren.' The full passive 'ist geboren worden' is reserved for the birth event itself. No imperative exists.
words.germany_context: Every German form asks for Geburtsdatum and Geburtsort. Bring a sworn translation (beglaubigte Übersetzung) of your Turkish birth certificate for the Bürgeramt and Standesamt.

example_sentences.en: We're getting married in the summer.
She married a German.

cloze.en: When are you getting married?

words.notes: Takes a plain accusative, no preposition: 'Er heiratet sie' — never 'mit ihr'.
words.germany_context: Only the ceremony at the Standesamt is legally valid in Germany. A religious or symbolic wedding has no legal effect on its own.

example_sentences.en: I cancelled my contract.

example_sentences.de: Sie kündigt zum Ende des Monats.
example_sentences.en: She's quitting at the end of the month.

cloze.de: Wir müssen die Wohnung drei Monate vorher ___.
cloze.en: We have to give notice on the flat three months in advance.

words.notes: 'Etwas kündigen' (Akkusativ) = cancel a contract; 'jemandem kündigen' (Dativ) = to fire someone. The noun is 'die Kündigung'.
words.germany_context: German contracts renew automatically unless you cancel. A Kündigung normally has to be in writing, and a flat requires three months' notice.

example_sentences.en: Please keep breathing calmly.

example_sentences.de: Nach dem Laufen atme ich schwer.
example_sentences.en: After running I breathe heavily.

cloze.en: The baby breathes very quietly.

words.notes: The stem ends in -tm, so an extra -e- is inserted: du atmest, er atmet, ihr atmet.

example_sentences.en: The baby is crying again.
She cried for joy.

cloze.en: Why are you crying?

words.notes: Careful: 'weinen' is to cry, 'der Wein' is wine. Different words, same sound.

example_sentences.en: We laughed a lot.
He's laughing about my accent.

cloze.de: Alle ___, aber ich verstehe den Witz nicht.
cloze.en: Everyone is laughing, but I don't get the joke.

words.notes: 'Über etwas lachen' (Akkusativ) = to laugh about something.

example_sentences.en: She smiles in a friendly way.
Say cheese!

cloze.en: The shop assistant only smiled briefly.

words.notes: 'Lächeln' = smile, 'lachen' = laugh. Verbs in -eln drop the e in the ich-form: ich lächle.
words.germany_context: Strangers in Germany rarely smile at each other on the street or in shops. It isn't unfriendliness, just a different norm — don't read it as rejection.

example_sentences.en: Please don't shout so loudly!

example_sentences.de: Das Kind hat die ganze Nacht geschrien.
example_sentences.en: The child screamed all night.

cloze.en: Why is he shouting like that?

words.notes: Strong: schrie, geschrien — note there is no -e- before the -n in the participle.
words.germany_context: Ruhezeiten are real rules, not suggestions: usually 22:00–06:00, plus all day Sunday. Loud noise gets you a complaint from the neighbours or a visit from the Ordnungsamt.

example_sentences.de: Sie flüstert mir etwas ins Ohr.
example_sentences.en: She whispers something in my ear.
Everyone whispers in the museum.

cloze.en: Why are you whispering?

words.notes: Verbs in -ern keep the e in the ich-form: ich flüstere.
